answer:
**KERNEL is the biggest risk by measured volume, but most of its fatal log volume came from a single month (June 2005). APP has a steadier fatal level and needs attention almost as urgently.**

## Observed Facts
Data Scope: BGL Dataset, full range 2005-06-03 to 2006-01-04, 4,747,963 Log Entries [E1]. No filters unless stated.

| Priority | Component | All Log Entries [E2] | FATAL-level Log Entries [E4] | Pattern over time (FATAL only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **KERNEL** | 4,324,651 | 626,450 | Spike: 535,054 in Jun 2005, then 6,244–28,909 per month from Jul to Dec 2005 [E6] |
| 2 | **APP** | 228,536 | 228,536 (every APP entry is FATAL) | Ongoing: 32,530–52,757 per month from Aug to Dec 2005 [E7] |
| 3 | LINKCARD | 1,170 | 206 | not trended |
| — | MMCS | 88,930 | 3 | almost no FATAL entries |

- KERNEL and APP together account for nearly all of the 855,195 FATAL-level Log Entries in BGL [E4].
- The alert tags with the most entries are all kernel or application ones: KERNDTLB 152,734, KERNSTOR 63,491, APPSEV 49,651, KERNMNTF 31,531, KERNTERM 23,338 (full BGL scope) [E5].
- From August to December 2005, APP logged more FATAL entries than KERNEL every month. In September 2005, for example, APP had 52,757 [E7] and KERNEL had 28,909 [E6].
- January 2006 only covers data up to 2006-01-04, so its low counts don't show an improvement [E1].

## Hypotheses
- KERNEL ranks first mainly because of the June 2005 spike. It may have been a single event that has since passed, though it still produced thousands of FATAL entries a month afterwards.
- APP may be the bigger ongoing risk, because its FATAL volume stayed high from August to December instead of dropping.
- Some of these counts may be one failure repeated across many log lines. High volume doesn't necessarily mean many separate problems.

## Unknowns
- Log Entry counts are not incidents. The logs can't tell me how many separate failures occurred.
- The logs can't establish financial loss, downtime, or customer or job impact for any Component.
- I don't know whether the June 2005 KERNEL spike was fixed or simply stopped being logged.

## Next Step
Assign KERNEL first, and APP alongside it as a close second, for engineering review:
1. KERNEL: find the cause of the June 2005 spike and check whether the KERNDTLB and KERNSTOR alert types are still active.
2. APP: break down its steady FATAL volume by alert type and node to see whether a few sources produce most of it.
